q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH₂OH is:
x: A three-carbon chain with –OH on C-1 is propan-1-ol. Propan-2-ol has –OH on the middle carbon; propanal and propanone are carbonyl compounds.

q: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃COH (tert-butyl alcohol) is:
x: The longest chain containing the –OH carbon has three carbons; C-2 carries both the –OH and a methyl group, so the name is 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

q: Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃, is classified as a:
x: The carbon carrying –OH is bonded to two other carbon atoms, so propan-2-ol is a secondary alcohol. It has only one –OH group, so it is monohydric.

q: Ethane-1,2-diol (ethylene glycol), HOCH₂CH₂OH, is an example of a:
x: It contains two –OH groups on different carbon atoms, so it is a dihydric alcohol (a diol). Glycerol, with three –OH groups, is trihydric.

q: The IUPAC name of glycerol, HOCH₂CH(OH)CH₂OH, is:
x: Glycerol has a three-carbon chain with one –OH on each carbon, so it is propane-1,2,3-triol.

q: The oxygen atom of the –OH group in an alcohol such as methanol is:
x: The oxygen has two bonds (to C and H) and two lone pairs, four electron pairs in all, so it is sp³ hybridised, giving a bent C–O–H arrangement.

q: Ethanol (M = 46) boils at 78 °C, while propane (M = 44) boils at −42 °C. The main reason is that ethanol:
x: The –OH groups of neighbouring ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other, and extra energy is needed to break these. Propane has only weak London forces.

q: Which alcohol is the least soluble in water?
x: All alcohols hydrogen bond with water through –OH, but the non-polar alkyl part grows with chain length. Hexan-1-ol has the largest hydrocarbon part, so it is the least soluble.

q: How many structurally different alcohols have the molecular formula C₄H₁₀O?
x: The alcohols are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol: four. Seven is the total only if the three isomeric ethers are also counted.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain has four carbons. Numbering must give the –OH the lowest number, so –OH is on C-2 and the methyl on C-3: 3-methylbutan-2-ol.

q: When a small piece of sodium is added to ethanol, the gas given off is:
x: 2C₂H₅OH + 2Na → 2C₂H₅ONa + H₂. Sodium replaces the hydrogen of the –OH group, forming sodium ethoxide and hydrogen gas.

q: Ethanol reacts with phosphorus pentachloride (PCl₅). The products are:
x: C₂H₅OH + PCl₅ → C₂H₅Cl + POCl₃ + HCl. H₃PO₃ is a product with PCl₃, and SO₂ is a product with thionyl chloride.

q: Thionyl chloride (SOCl₂) is often preferred for converting an alcohol to an alkyl chloride because:
o: It gives an alkene and an alkyl chloride together
It needs no reaction with the –OH group
It produces water as the only by-product
The by-products SO₂ and HCl are gases and escape, leaving a purer product
x: ROH + SOCl₂ → RCl + SO₂ + HCl. Both by-products are gases that leave the mixture, so the alkyl chloride is easy to obtain pure.

q: Lucas reagent, used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, is:
x: Lucas reagent is concentrated hydrochloric acid with anhydrous zinc chloride. It converts alcohols into insoluble alkyl chlorides at different rates, seen as cloudiness.

q: Which alcohol gives cloudiness immediately with Lucas reagent at room temperature?
x: Tertiary alcohols such as 2-methylpropan-2-ol react at once; secondary alcohols like butan-2-ol take a few minutes; primary alcohols show no cloudiness at room temperature.

q: Ethanol is heated under reflux with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. The main organic product is:
x: A primary alcohol is oxidised first to an aldehyde and, with excess oxidant under reflux, on to the carboxylic acid: ethanol → ethanal → ethanoic acid.

q: Compound X, C₃H₈O, is oxidised by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ to a ketone. X is:
x: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones: propan-2-ol gives propanone. Propan-1-ol gives propanal then propanoic acid; methoxyethane is an ether and propanal is not C₃H₈O.

q: 2-Methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ under ordinary conditions because:
o: It has no hydrogen atom on the carbon carrying the –OH group
x: Oxidation of an alcohol removes the H from the –OH carbon. In a tertiary alcohol this carbon is bonded to three carbons and has no H, so it resists mild oxidation.

q: When acidified potassium dichromate oxidises a primary or secondary alcohol, its colour changes from:
x: Orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced to green Cr³⁺ as the alcohol is oxidised. Purple to colourless is the change seen with acidified KMnO₄.

q: A small piece of sodium reacts with ethanol, but much more gently than with water. This is because:
o: Ethanol has no O–H bond, so sodium can react only with its C–H bonds
Ethanol molecules are lighter than water molecules, so they collide less often
Sodium does not react with ethanol at all but only dissolves in it
Ethanol is a weaker acid than water, so it gives up its O–H hydrogen less readily
x: The electron-releasing ethyl group makes the O–H bond of ethanol less polar than in water, so ethanol is a slightly weaker acid. It still gives sodium ethoxide and hydrogen, only more slowly. Ethanol (M = 46) is heavier than water (M = 18).

q: 9.2 g of ethanol (C₂H₅OH, M = 46) reacts completely with excess sodium. The volume of hydrogen formed at STP is (1 mol gas = 22.4 dm³):
x: Moles of ethanol = 9.2/46 = 0.2. 2C₂H₅OH gives 1 H₂, so H₂ = 0.1 mol = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³. Using a 1 : 1 ratio wrongly gives 4.48 dm³.

q: The reaction of an alcohol with a carboxylic acid in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to give a sweet-smelling product is called:
x: Alcohol + carboxylic acid ⇌ ester + water is esterification. Saponification and hydrolysis are the reverse type of process, breaking an ester down.

q: Ethanol reacts with ethanoic acid (acetic acid) in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄. The ester formed is:
x: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O. The ethyl part comes from the alcohol and the ethanoate part from the acid, so the ester is ethyl ethanoate (ethyl acetate).

q: In the preparation of an ester from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid, concentrated H₂SO₄:
x: Concentrated H₂SO₄ is the acid catalyst for esterification (it also takes up the water formed). It does not oxidise, reduce or neutralise the reactants.

q: Ethanol reacts with ethanoyl chloride (acetyl chloride) at room temperature: CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → ? + HCl. The organic product is:
x: The C₂H₅O– group of ethanol replaces Cl on the acyl chloride, giving the ester CH₃COOC₂H₅, and HCl is released; no acid catalyst is needed. Ethoxyethane comes from ethanol with conc. H₂SO₄ or from the Williamson synthesis.

q: Sodium ethoxide is heated with bromoethane: C₂H₅ONa + C₂H₅Br → ? + NaBr. The organic product is:
x: This is the Williamson synthesis: the ethoxide ion replaces Br in bromoethane, giving the ether C₂H₅OC₂H₅ (ethoxyethane) and NaBr.

q: The IUPAC name of the ester CH₃COOCH₃ is:
x: CH₃COO– comes from ethanoic acid (ethanoate) and –CH₃ from methanol (methyl), so the ester is methyl ethanoate. Ethyl methanoate would be HCOOC₂H₅.

q: Which statement about the esterification of ethanol with ethanoic acid is correct?
o: It goes to completion quickly without any catalyst
It is a reversible reaction that reaches equilibrium
The alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde
x: Esterification is slow and reversible (ester + water can hydrolyse back), so an acid catalyst is used and the mixture reaches equilibrium. Water, not hydrogen, is the by-product.

q: Many simple esters, such as those found in fruits, are best known for their:
x: Low-molecular-mass esters are volatile liquids with pleasant fruity smells; they give many fruits and flowers their odours and are used as flavourings.

q: When ethanoic acid labelled with ¹⁸O only in its –OH group reacts with ordinary ethanol to form an ester, the ¹⁸O ends up in:
o: Both the ester and the water equally
Neither, as it escapes as gas
x: In esterification the acid loses its –OH and the alcohol loses only H from its –OH. So the labelled –OH of the acid joins the H of ethanol to form water, and the ester has the alcohol's oxygen.

q: Which pair of reagents gives methoxyethane, CH₃OC₂H₅, by the Williamson synthesis?
x: CH₃O⁻ from sodium methoxide replaces Br in C₂H₅Br, giving CH₃OC₂H₅. Bromomethane would give dimethyl ether and bromoethane with ethoxide gives diethyl ether.

q: The molecular formula of phenol is:
x: Phenol has an –OH group bonded directly to a benzene ring: C₆H₅OH. C₆H₅CH₂OH is benzyl alcohol and C₆H₁₁OH is cyclohexanol.

q: Phenol is also known by the common name:
x: Phenol is commonly called carbolic acid. Wood spirit is methanol, picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol and glycol is ethane-1,2-diol.

q: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol mainly because:
o: Phenol has a higher molar mass
The ethoxide ion is stabilised by resonance
The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance with the benzene ring
x: In the phenoxide ion the negative charge spreads into the ring by resonance, which stabilises it, so phenol loses H⁺ more easily. The ethoxide ion has no such resonance.

q: Phenol is shaken with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The products are:
o: No products, as no reaction occurs
x: Phenol is acidic enough to be neutralised by NaOH: C₆H₅OH + NaOH → C₆H₅ONa + H₂O. Hydrogen is formed only with sodium metal.

q: Which reagent gives carbon dioxide with ethanoic acid but not with phenol?
x: Phenol is a weaker acid than carbonic acid, so it cannot release CO₂ from NaHCO₃, while ethanoic acid can. Sodium metal gives hydrogen, not CO₂.

q: The compound CH₃C₆H₄OH in which the –CH₃ group is next to the –OH group is named:
x: Numbering starts at the carbon carrying –OH (C-1); the adjacent carbon is C-2, so it is 2-methylphenol (o-cresol). Benzyl alcohol is C₆H₅CH₂OH.

q: Which of the following is NOT a phenol?
x: In C₆H₅CH₂OH (benzyl alcohol) the –OH is on a CH₂ side-chain carbon, not on the ring, so it is an aromatic alcohol. The others have –OH directly on the benzene ring.

q: The carbon atom bonded to the –OH group in phenol is:
x: This carbon is part of the benzene ring, whose carbons are all sp² hybridised. In an alcohol such as ethanol, the carbon carrying –OH is sp³.

q: Unlike ethanol, phenol does not readily form a chloride when treated with HCl. This is because in phenol:
o: The C–O bond has partial double-bond character due to resonance
The oxygen has no lone pairs
x: A lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, giving the C–O bond partial double-bond character. This bond is hard to break, so the –OH is not easily replaced.

q: The correct order of decreasing acidity is:
x: Ethanoic acid is the strongest (it releases CO₂ from NaHCO₃; phenol does not). Phenol is more acidic than water, and ethanol is slightly less acidic than water.

q: Which of the following is the strongest acid?
x: The electron-withdrawing –NO₂ group spreads the negative charge of the phenoxide ion further, stabilising it, so 4-nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol. An electron-releasing –CH₃ group makes the phenol weaker.

q: Phenol reacts with bromine water at room temperature to give:
x: The strongly activating –OH group makes the ring so reactive that bromine water substitutes all three ortho and para positions, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

q: The precipitate formed when bromine water is added to aqueous phenol is:
x: 2,4,6-Tribromophenol is insoluble in water and separates as a white precipitate while the bromine colour disappears. Violet is the colour phenol gives with FeCl₃.

q: In electrophilic substitution, the –OH group of phenol directs the incoming electrophile to the:
x: The –OH group donates electron density into the ring by resonance, mainly at the ortho and para positions, so it is an ortho, para-director.

q: Phenol reacts with bromine without a catalyst, but benzene needs a FeBr₃ catalyst. The reason is that the –OH group:
o: Reacts with bromine to make Br⁺ directly
Releases electrons into the ring through a lone pair on oxygen
x: A lone pair on oxygen is delocalised into the ring, raising its electron density, so the ring attracts electrophiles strongly. The –OH group is therefore activating.

q: Phenol is treated with dilute nitric acid at room temperature. The main products are:
x: Because phenol is so reactive, dilute HNO₃ is enough to nitrate it, giving a mixture of ortho- and para-nitrophenol. Concentrated acid is needed for trinitration.

q: Phenol is treated with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid. The main product is:
x: Under strongly nitrating conditions all three ortho and para positions are substituted, giving 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, known as picric acid.

q: Phenol reacts with bromine dissolved in a non-polar solvent such as CS₂ at low temperature. The main products are:
x: In a non-polar solvent at low temperature the reaction is milder, so only one bromine enters, at the ortho or para position. In water, all three positions are substituted.

q: In the nitration of an aromatic ring, the electrophile that attacks the ring is:
x: The nitronium ion, NO₂⁺, is the electrophile. It is positive and attacks the electron-rich ring; NO₃⁻ and NO₂⁻ are negative and are not electrophiles.

q: How many moles of Br₂ react completely with 0.5 mol of phenol to form 2,4,6-tribromophenol?
x: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr. Each phenol needs 3 Br₂, so 0.5 × 3 = 1.5 mol. A 1 : 1 ratio would wrongly give 0.5 mol; 3.0 mol is the amount for 1 mol of phenol.

q: 4-Methylphenol is treated with excess bromine water. The main product is:
x: The –OH group directs to its ortho and para positions. The para position is already taken by –CH₃, so excess bromine fills both ortho positions (2 and 6).

q: Neutral iron(III) chloride solution is added to aqueous phenol. The colour seen is:
x: Phenols form a coloured complex with Fe³⁺, typically violet. Alcohols such as ethanol give no such colour, so this is a standard test for phenol.

q: Which test can distinguish ethanol from phenol?
o: Adding a small piece of sodium
Adding water and checking for mixing
Burning a small sample in air
x: Phenol gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃ while ethanol does not. Both compounds react with sodium to give hydrogen, so sodium cannot tell them apart.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes phenol from ethanol?
o: Ethanol reacts with aqueous NaOH to form a salt; phenol does not
Only ethanol gives hydrogen with sodium
Phenol reacts with aqueous NaOH to form a salt; ethanol does not
x: Phenol is acidic enough to form sodium phenoxide with NaOH; ethanol is too weak an acid. Both react with sodium and both form hydrogen bonds.

q: Ethanol, but not phenol, gives a yellow precipitate when warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide. This precipitate is:
x: Ethanol contains the CH₃CH(OH)– unit and gives the iodoform test, forming yellow CHI₃. Phenol does not have this unit and gives no iodoform.

q: A colourless compound in water decolourises bromine water at once and gives a white precipitate. The compound is:
x: Phenol reacts with bromine water to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol. Saturated alcohols do not react with bromine water.

q: Which reaction is given by ethanol but NOT by phenol?
o: Giving a violet colour with FeCl₃
Forming a chloride with concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl₂
x: The C–O bond of an alcohol can be broken by HCl/ZnCl₂ to give an alkyl chloride, but phenol's C–O bond has partial double-bond character and is not replaced. The last two reactions are given by phenol only.

q: Which reagent reacts with both ethanol and phenol?
x: Both have an O–H bond and give hydrogen with sodium (forming sodium ethoxide and sodium phenoxide). The other three reagents react with phenol only.

q: At room temperature, pure phenol and pure ethanol are respectively:
o: A colourless crystalline solid and a colourless liquid
A colourless liquid and a white solid
A violet solid and a yellow liquid
x: Phenol melts at about 41 °C, so it is a colourless crystalline solid at room temperature (it turns pink in air). Ethanol is a colourless liquid.

q: Compound X, C₇H₈O, gives hydrogen with sodium, gives no colour with neutral FeCl₃ and does not dissolve in aqueous NaOH. X is:
x: No FeCl₃ colour and no reaction with NaOH rule out the phenols. Reaction with sodium shows an O–H group, which methoxybenzene (an ether) lacks. So X is the alcohol C₆H₅CH₂OH.

q: Y gives a violet colour with neutral FeCl₃ and a white precipitate with bromine water. Z gives neither, but turns acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ from orange to green. Y and Z could be:
x: The FeCl₃ and bromine water results show Y is a phenol. Z is oxidised by dichromate, so it is a primary or secondary alcohol such as ethanol; tertiary 2-methylpropan-2-ol is not oxidised.
